---
title: "Balancing an elite program and a pre-breeding program"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

The [introgression article](introgression.html) put exotic germplasm straight
into the elite crossing block through bridging crosses. Many programs
instead run a separate **pre-breeding** program. It starts from elite ×
exotic crosses and improves them by its own cycles of selection, and only its
best lines are passed to the elite program. A breeder with a fixed budget
then has to decide how to split it between the two programs.

This article compares the two approaches with a `sim_set()`: two
`alphasim_program()` specs, run on the same replicates and ranked together.
It also makes the exotic germplasm more realistic than the introgression
article did. Here the exotics start well below the elite pool, as wild
soybean would.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(AlphaSimR)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Shared pieces

Both programs start from the same two pools. Half the founders are selected
*for* yield for eight generations (the elite pool). The other half are
selected *against* it for four generations, which stands in for wild
germplasm that is poorly adapted. A few small helpers keep the programs
short:

```{r}
make_pools <- function(founders) {
  elite <- founders[1:30]
  exotic <- founders[31:60]
  for (g in 1:8) elite <- self(randCross(selectInd(setPheno(elite), 10), nCrosses = 30, nProgeny = 2))
  for (g in 1:4) exotic <- self(randCross(selectInd(setPheno(exotic), 10, selectTop = FALSE), nCrosses = 30))
  list(elite = self(self(elite)), exotic = self(self(exotic)))
}
# Three generations of selfing, then a two-rep yield trial.
advance <- function(pop) setPheno(self(self(pop)), reps = 2)
# n crosses between random members of a and b.
cross_to <- function(a, b, n) {
  hybridCross(a, b, crossPlan = cbind(sample(nInd(a), n, TRUE), sample(nInd(b), n, TRUE)))
}
```

Every program grows 400 lines a cycle, in families of 10, and keeps 15
parents. `share` is the fraction of those 400 lines spent on exotic
material, and three parent slots are kept for the best exotic-derived lines,
as in the introgression article. The budget is the same for every design.

## Two ways to use the exotic share

**Bridging** makes new elite × exotic crosses every cycle, backcrosses them
once to elite, and offers the best to the elite program:

```{r}
bridging <- function(founders, SP, share, n_lines = 400, per_cross = 10, n_parents = 15,
                     reserved = 3, cycles = 15) {
  pools <- make_pools(founders)
  tracker <- asr_tracker(pools$elite)
  parents <- selectInd(setPheno(pools$elite, reps = 4), n_parents)
  for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
    n_side <- round(share * n_lines / per_cross)
    lines <- advance(self(randCross(parents, nCrosses = n_lines / per_cross - n_side), nProgeny = per_cross))
    if (n_side > 0) {
      bc1 <- cross_to(cross_to(parents, pools$exotic, n_side), parents, n_side)
      side <- advance(self(bc1, nProgeny = per_cross))
      parents <- c(selectInd(lines, n_parents - reserved), selectInd(side, reserved))
    } else {
      parents <- selectInd(lines, n_parents)
    }
    tracker$record(parents, year = cycle * 4, released_lines = selectInd(lines, 3))
  }
  asr_summary(tracker)
}
```

**Pre-breeding** starts the same way, but then keeps its own population.
Each cycle it crosses its own best lines, three quarters among themselves and
one quarter back to elite parents. It offers its best lines to the elite
program, which by then have had several cycles of improvement:

```{r}
prebreeding <- function(founders, SP, share, n_lines = 400, per_cross = 10, n_parents = 15,
                        reserved = 3, cycles = 15) {
  pools <- make_pools(founders)
  tracker <- asr_tracker(pools$elite)
  parents <- selectInd(setPheno(pools$elite, reps = 4), n_parents)
  pb_parents <- NULL
  for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
    n_side <- round(share * n_lines / per_cross)
    lines <- advance(self(randCross(parents, nCrosses = n_lines / per_cross - n_side), nProgeny = per_cross))
    if (n_side > 0) {
      pb <- if (is.null(pb_parents)) {
        cross_to(cross_to(parents, pools$exotic, n_side), parents, n_side)    # first cycle: elite x exotic, BC1
      } else {
        c(randCross(pb_parents, nCrosses = n_side - n_side %/% 4), cross_to(pb_parents, parents, n_side %/% 4))
      }
      side <- advance(self(pb, nProgeny = per_cross))
      pb_parents <- selectInd(side, 10)
      parents <- c(selectInd(lines, n_parents - reserved), selectInd(side, reserved))
    } else {
      parents <- selectInd(lines, n_parents)
    }
    tracker$record(parents, year = cycle * 4, released_lines = selectInd(lines, 3))
  }
  asr_summary(tracker)
}
```

The two functions differ only in where `side` comes from.

## One study, two specs

`sim_set()` holds several specs, and `sim_map()` runs the same tuning call
on each. Both use the same founders and the same replicate seeds, so every
comparison is paired, between strategies as well as between shares.

```{r}
founders <- asr_founders(n_founders = 60, n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 150, qtl_per_chr = 15)
set <- sim_set(
  bridging = alphasim_program(bridging, share = tune(), founders = founders),
  prebreeding = alphasim_program(prebreeding, share = tune(), founders = founders)
)
set <- sim_map(set, "tune_grid", resamples = sim_replicates(15, seed = 1),
               grid = data.frame(share = c(0, 0.15, 0.3)),
               metrics = sim_metric_set(release_gain, genetic_variance),
               control = control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE))
rank_results(set, rank_metric = "release_gain")[, c("wflow_id", "rank", "parameters", "release_gain",
                                                    "release_gain_se", "genetic_variance")]
```

`rank_results()` puts every design of every spec in one table, with its
settings in `parameters`. The two
`share = 0` rows are the same elite-only program run through each spec, and
they agree exactly, because both ran on the same seeds.

## Over time

`extract_sim_result()` pulls out one spec's results, so trajectories can be
collected from each and combined:

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean genetic value of the parents over 60 years. Parent sets that include bridging lines stay below the elite-only program for most of the period; pre-breeding with 30 percent of the budget dips early, then passes it after about 30 years."}
traj <- rbind(
  transform(collect_trajectories(extract_sim_result(set, "bridging")), strategy = "Bridging"),
  transform(collect_trajectories(extract_sim_result(set, "prebreeding")), strategy = "Pre-breeding")
)
avg <- aggregate(mean ~ strategy + share + year, data = traj, FUN = mean)
avg$design <- ifelse(avg$share == 0, "Elite only", paste0(avg$strategy, ", ", 100 * avg$share, "%"))
avg <- avg[!(avg$share == 0 & avg$strategy == "Pre-breeding"), ]

ggplot(avg, aes(year, mean, colour = design)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Elite only" = "black", "Bridging, 15%" = "#FDBB84",
                                 "Bridging, 30%" = "#E45756", "Pre-breeding, 15%" = "#9ECAE9",
                                 "Pre-breeding, 30%" = "#4C78A8")) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean genetic value of parents\n(elite genetic SDs)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Pre-breeding lines catch up; raw bridging lines lag")
```

```{r}
pre <- extract_sim_result(set, "prebreeding")
m <- collect_metrics(pre, type = "wide")
compare_designs(pre, m$.config[m$share == 0], m$.config[m$share == 0.3], metric = "release_gain")
```

## What it shows

* **Both ways of using exotics beat elite only.** After 15 cycles, every
  design that spends part of the budget on exotic material releases better
  lines than the elite-only program. Pre-breeding with 30% of the budget
  ranks first, about half a genetic SD ahead of elite only (the paired
  comparison above). The other three are within about one standard error of
  each other.
* **Pre-breeding lines earn their parent slots.** The plot follows the mean
  of the whole parent set, including the three reserved slots. Pre-breeding
  lines improve cycle after cycle, so with 30% of the budget the parent set
  catches up after about 20 years and pulls ahead after 30. Fresh bridging
  lines start from germplasm far below the elite every cycle, so they pull
  the parent mean down for most of the 60 years. They still add useful
  alleles, which is why the lines released from the elite crosses gain.
* **Read diversity metrics with care.** Bridging finishes with by far the
  highest `genetic_variance` among its parents, but most of that is the gap
  between three poor bridging lines and twelve elite lines, not variation
  the elite program can use right away. A metric is only as good as what it
  measures. Here, genetic variance among the *elite* lines, or the gain of
  later cycles, would be fairer measures of useful diversity.
* **The answer depends on the germplasm.** In the introgression article,
  where exotics were unselected rather than poorly adapted, the cost of
  bridging was smaller. How far below the elite your exotic sources are is
  the assumption to get right. A scenario over it, for example through the
  number of generations of selection against yield in `make_pools()`, is
  the natural next study.

## Make it yours

* Make `reserved`, the quarter of pre-breeding crosses that go back to
  elite, and the number of pre-breeding parents all `tune()` arguments, and
  search them with `tune_bayes()`.
* Give the pre-breeding program its own, cheaper trials (one rep, one
  location), and move the money saved into more lines.
* Add a third spec to the set, such as a program that runs bridging and
  pre-breeding side by side, and rank all three with `rank_results()`.
* Use your own elite and exotic marker data through
  `asr_founders(haplotypes = )`.
